summary: This unit teaches you to manage yourself at work: to know your strengths and weaknesses, set goals and a development plan, be on time and reliable, take responsibility, control your feelings, accept feedback, look after your health and money, and keep learning as the job changes. These habits make a villa or hotel worker whom supervisors trust and promote.

blocks.p: Self-management means taking charge of your own work, your time and your behaviour, so that people can trust you to do a good job without watching you all the time. In a villa, hotel, restaurant or attraction, supervisors cannot be everywhere. The workers who are given more training, better shifts and promotion are the ones who manage themselves.

This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. Most of it is about habits. Habits are built by practice, so use every day at the Centre as a chance to practise: arrive early, plan your tasks, take feedback well and finish what you start.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: a theory paper with multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, and two group practical tasks: a personal SWOT and development plan with a group poster, and a role play of a busy shift at a villa. In the role play each member handles real situations: reporting sickness, a rude co-worker, a mistake on a bill, feedback, and a request outside your role. Use made-up names and details.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In the practical tasks, share only what you are happy to share. Your self-assessment is private to you, your partner and the assessor.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Know yourself and reflect on your work

blocks.p: You cannot improve what you have not noticed. Self-management starts with honest self-knowledge: what you do well, what you find hard, and how others see you.

head: Topic
Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: What they are
Things you do well
Things you find hard, avoid, or often get wrong
Examples in hospitality
Staying calm and friendly when it is busy
Neat, careful work
Good memory for guests' names
Forgetting orders when the restaurant is full
Getting nervous when speaking to a group
Being late after a night shift
What to do
Use them every day and mention them at interviews.
Choose one at a time, make a plan, practise and ask for feedback.

blocks.p: A weakness is not a failure. It is the next thing to learn. Workers who pretend they have no weaknesses never improve.

ul: **Think** honestly about your own work: which tasks go well and which ones you avoid.
**Ask** your supervisor and a co-worker you trust for honest feedback. Do not ask only people who will say what you want to hear.
**Look** at your appraisal, guest comments and the results of room checks.

Write it as a **SWOT**: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities (chances to learn or move up, such as a course or a new section opening) and threats (things that could hold you back, such as transport problems or tiredness).

blocks.h: Reflecting at the end of a shift

blocks.p: **Reflecting** means looking back so that you learn. At the end of a shift, ask yourself three questions:

ol: What will I do differently tomorrow?

blocks.p: Do not use reflection to judge others or to feel bad. It is about your work only. Write a line or two in a notebook; after a few weeks you will see patterns.

blocks.note: Example: a trainee server notices that she forgets drinks orders when three tables sit at once. Her plan: write each order down, repeat it back to the guest, and ask a senior server how she keeps track. After three weeks she asks for feedback again.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Motivation** is the drive inside you that makes you want to work hard and do well, without being pushed. It is stronger when your work has a purpose, such as a goal you chose. Remind yourself why you are working: a qualification, helping your family, a promotion, or pride in what you do.
Goals give you direction and let you see progress. Without them, work becomes one day after another. Goals belong to you: they are not only for managers.

head: Type
Time
Examples for a trainee in hospitality
rows: Short-term goal
Days to a few months
Make up a villa room to standard in 30 minutes within three months
Be on time every day this month
Finish the Food Handler's Permit
Long-term goal
A year or more
Be a team leader in housekeeping within two years
Complete NVQ-J Level 3
Become a head cook in five years

blocks.p: Good goals are clear and measurable and have a date (the SMART method). Short-term goals are the steps toward the long-term goal.
A **personal development plan** is a written plan of the skills and training you will work on, and by when.

head: Part of the plan
Example
rows: Goal
Within three months, I will make up a villa room to standard in 30 minutes.
Steps
Watch an experienced room attendant; practise each day; ask my supervisor to check three rooms a week.
Help I need
A mentor; time on the rota to practise; the room checklist.
Date
15 February, with a progress check each month.
Long-term goal
Within two years, be a team leader in housekeeping: finish NVQ-J Level 2, do the Team Jamaica training, ask to help train new staff.

ul: Look at your plan regularly: once a month is a good habit. Tick off what you have done and change what is not working.
A goal that is never looked at again is only a wish.
Keep **copies of your certificates** (NVQ-J, Food Handler's Permit, Team Jamaica, first aid) in a folder, and the originals safe at home.
Employers ask to see your training when they promote or hire, and keeping records shows you are organised.
Keep a list of the dates and what you learnt, and update your CV after each course.

head: Help
What it is
rows: Induction
The first training new staff get about the property, its rules and their job. Take notes.
Mentor
A more experienced worker who guides and advises you as you learn.
Appraisal
A regular meeting where your supervisor reviews your work with you and you agree new goals.
Courses
Short courses such as first aid, a language, customer care or food safety.

sections.title: Being reliable: attendance, punctuality and planning

blocks.p: Hotels and villas plan shifts so that there are enough staff for the guests. If you are late or absent, rooms are not ready, guests wait and your co-workers must do your work as well as their own. **Reliable** workers can be counted on to turn up and do the job well every time.

ul: Being punctual means being **in uniform and ready to work** at the start of your shift, not walking in at that time.
Plan your journey with extra time: route taxis break down and roads flood. Arrive 10 to 15 minutes early.
Get your things ready the night before: uniform, shoes, name badge, money for fare.
If you will be late despite your best efforts, **phone before** your start time, say why and say when you will arrive.

flow: Call your supervisor as early as possible, before your shift, as the property's rules say
Say that you are sick, and when you expect to return
Do not send a message through a co-worker unless the rules allow it
Get a doctor's note if the rules ask for one
Tell your supervisor when you are better, and ask what you missed

ul: Never just stay away without telling anyone. This is one of the quickest ways to lose a job.
If you have something that could spread, such as a stomach illness, do not handle food or guests' rooms until you are well. Tell your supervisor.

ol: Look at your task list or room list when you arrive.
Put urgent and time-critical tasks first, such as rooms for early arrivals or breakfast set-up.
Then do tasks that take the longest or involve guests' requests.
Leave tasks that can wait, such as restocking the store, for quiet times.
Leave time for checks, breaks and unexpected jobs.
If something new and urgent arrives, tell your supervisor what you were doing and ask which comes first.

blocks.note: Example: a villa attendant has 6 rooms to clean and a late check-out guest who leaves at 11 a.m. She plans the empty rooms first, then the late check-out room, then the pool-side towels. If a guest asks for extra towels, she does it at once, because a guest request is urgent.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A good **work ethic** means being honest, hard-working and reliable, whether or not the supervisor is watching.
**Integrity** means being honest even when no one would find out: recording the hours you actually worked, and not taking food, drinks or supplies without asking.
Keep promises. Do not say a job is done when it is not finished: this breaks the trust your supervisor has in you.
Do not take shortcuts that cheat guests or the business.

blocks.p: Everyone makes mistakes. **Accountability** means taking responsibility for what you do, including your mistakes. Hiding a mistake makes it worse: it can cost the business money, upset guests and make people stop trusting you.

flow: Make the situation safe
Tell your supervisor quickly and honestly
Apologise to the guest or co-worker if they are affected
Help put it right by the property's procedure
Find out why it happened
Change what you do so that it does not happen again

ul: Do not blame the computer, the kitchen, a co-worker or the guest.
Keep guests' details private when you correct an error.
If you break something such as a glass, make the area safe first: use a brush and pan, not bare hands, then report it.
If you do not fully understand an instruction, **ask questions** until you are clear. Repeat it back: 'So you would like me to...?' Guessing causes mistakes.
**Procedures** (SOPs, standard operating procedures) are written steps for a task. They keep work safe and to the same standard every time. Follow them even when you think you know a faster way.
If you think a procedure can be improved, **suggest** it to your supervisor. Do not change it yourself. Say what you noticed, what you suggest and why.

blocks.p: **Initiative** means seeing what needs to be done and doing it without being told, within your role. Going beyond your authority means doing something that is not your job, that you have not been trained for, that costs money, or that needs a supervisor's decision.

head: Initiative (good)
Beyond your authority (not good)
rows: Putting a foot-wash basin and extra towels by the door when guests come back sandy from the beach
Adding chemicals to the pool when you have not been trained
Refilling empty salt shakers before service
Giving a guest a free meal without asking the manager
Clearing litter from the pool deck without being asked
Moving a guest to another room without approval
Telling your supervisor the towel stock is low
Using your own money to buy supplies and charging guests

blocks.note: A test: Is it part of my job? Am I trained for it? Is it safe? Does it cost money or break a rule? If the answer to the last question is yes, or you are unsure of any, ask your supervisor first.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Pride in your work** means doing a job well even when no one is watching, and checking it before you leave it, for example looking once more around a room you have cleaned.

**Self-discipline** means doing what you should do rather than what you feel like doing: keeping your phone in your locker during your shift, not taking longer breaks when the supervisor is away, and finishing hard tasks first.
Follow the property's **code of conduct**: the rules on behaviour, dress and how to treat guests.
Do not post about guests, co-workers or problems at work. It can break guests' privacy and harm the business.
Do not post photos of guests or of private areas of a villa, even if the guest is a celebrity. Respect a guest's wish to keep their stay private.
Check the property's social media rules. Your posts show who you are as a worker.

blocks.p: Hospitality is often hot, loud and fast. Guests can be tired, upset or rude, and co-workers have bad days. **Emotional intelligence** is being able to understand and control your own feelings and to understand other people's. It is one of the skills employers value most.

flow: Notice the signs: hot face, fast heartbeat, a raised voice
Pause before you react
Take a slow breath and stay professional
Keep your voice low and polite and listen to the whole complaint
Do not take it personally: the guest is usually upset about the situation
Offer what you can do; get your supervisor if you cannot calm it

ul: Do not be rude back, walk away from the guest, or argue. Never cry or shout at the guest.
If you are shaking or too upset to continue, ask your supervisor to take over and take a short break.

blocks.h: When a co-worker makes you angry

ul: Do not argue in front of guests, in the kitchen during service or in front of other staff.
Finish the task or service first. Then ask to talk **in private** when you are both calm.
Use 'I' statements: 'I felt upset when the glasses were left dirty, and I would like us to agree who clears them.' This is better than 'You never help.'
If it does not work, speak to your supervisor. Do not complain to guests or on social media.

blocks.p: A little stress keeps you alert. Too much, for too long, harms you and your work.

head: Signs of too much stress
Healthy ways to deal with it
rows: Trouble sleeping
Headaches
Snapping at people
Feeling tired all the time
Dreading going to work
Exercise, rest and enough sleep
Talking to someone you trust, such as a friend, family member or pastor
Planning your time and breaking big jobs into small steps
Taking proper breaks
Asking your supervisor for help

ul: Do **not** deal with stress with a lot of alcohol, skipping meals, or staying up late on your phone. These make you feel worse.
**Resilience** is being able to bounce back and keep going after a setback or a hard day. It grows when you look after yourself, learn from mistakes and ask for support.

blocks.p: Family problems, money worries or a loss can affect your work. If a problem is upsetting you, **talk to your supervisor in private** and say that you are having a difficult time. A good supervisor can often help with changed shifts or time off. Do not tell guests, and do not stay away without telling anyone. Keep working as well as you can in the meantime.

blocks.note: If you ever feel you cannot cope, or you are thinking of harming yourself, talk to a trusted adult, a doctor, or a counsellor straight away. Asking for help is a sign of strength.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Feedback** is information about how you are doing. **Constructive** feedback is meant to help you improve. You cannot always see your own mistakes, so feedback is one of the quickest ways to grow.

head: When
What to do
rows: Your supervisor praises your work
Thank them. Find out what they liked and keep doing it. Praise shows you your strengths and what the standard looks like.
Your supervisor criticises your work
Stay calm and listen to all of it
Do not argue or make excuses; do not say 'the last guest did not complain'
Remember it is about your work, not about you as a person
Ask questions: 'Can you show me how the corners should look?'
Say thank you for telling you
Nobody offers feedback
Ask for it. 'What is one thing I could do better?' shows that you want to improve.

flow: Listen without arguing
Ask what exactly must change
Make a plan
Practise
Ask for feedback again
Check your progress

blocks.p: Your supervisor says your work is good but you arrive five minutes late three days a week. Do not argue that the buses are late. Plan to leave home 20 minutes earlier, keep a note of your arrival times for a month, and ask to be checked again. Fix the problem and tell your supervisor you have done so.

blocks.note: Feedback from guests counts too. If a guest praises you, tell your supervisor, and say thank you to the guest. If a guest complains, listen and learn: the guest is telling you what to improve.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Hospitality work is physical and often has early, late or long shifts. A healthy worker works better and more safely.

head: Habit
Why it matters at work
What to do
rows: Sleep
Tired workers make mistakes and have accidents. A tired cook is more likely to cut a finger or burn food.
Most adults need about 7 to 9 hours a night. Keep a regular routine; do not stay up late before an early shift.
Food and water
Energy and concentration. Working in the heat without drinking can make you faint.
Eat proper meals, not just sweet drinks. Drink water often, especially outdoors at an attraction or beach.
Sun protection
Sunburn and heat exhaustion in outdoor jobs.
Use shade, a hat and sunscreen, and take your breaks in a cool place.
Exercise and rest
Helps with stress and strength for lifting and standing.
Take your days off to rest and to do something you enjoy.
Work-life balance
A healthy balance between work and time for rest, family and fun keeps you well.
Do not work every hour offered. Plan time for your own life.

ul: Shower every day. Use deodorant, but not strong perfume instead of washing.
Wear a clean, pressed uniform every shift. Never wear the same uniform all week.
Keep your nails short and clean. Keep hair neat and tied back if you work with food.
Wash your hands often with soap and water: at the start of the shift, after the toilet, before handling food, after handling rubbish.
Protects guests from germs and food from contamination, and makes a good impression.

blocks.p: If you are asked to work double shifts every day and you feel exhausted or unsafe, talk to your supervisor about your hours and your safety. Do not keep going in silence, and do not use energy drinks all day to stay awake. Mistakes made by tired workers can hurt people.
Money worries affect your sleep, your mood and your work. Planning how you spend your pay is part of self-management.

ol: Write down your pay and your fixed spending: rent, transport, food, phone credit.
Decide what you can save, even a small amount each pay day. A credit union account or a 'partner' (a savings group) can help you save regularly.
Spend on needs first, then on wants.
Keep your pay slip. Check it carefully. Report mistakes to payroll.

blocks.note: Never borrow from a lender who asks for very high interest or takes your card. If you are in difficulty, ask your supervisor or your credit union for advice.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Adapting to change and keeping your skills up to date

blocks.p: Change is normal in hospitality: new computer systems, new menus, new rules, new guests' needs and new safety procedures. A self-managed worker is **flexible**: willing to change the way they work when plans or conditions change.

flow: Go to the training and take notes
Practise when it is quiet
Ask for help when you are stuck
Help co-workers who find it hard
Tell your supervisor about any problem with the system

ul: Do not refuse to use it, wait for it to break, or let others do your work.
Keep a positive attitude. Complaining spreads and slows everyone down.

blocks.p: **Lifelong learning** means learning that carries on through your whole working life, not only at school. Guests' wishes and methods change, and workers who keep up are the ones who get promoted.

ul: Take short courses: first aid, customer care, a foreign language such as Spanish or French, food safety, computers.
Read about your trade, and learn from experienced staff and a mentor.
Keep your certificates safe, and update your personal development plan and your CV.
Tell your supervisor which training you would like. Ask about HEART/NSTA Trust courses and Team Jamaica training.

blocks.note: Keeping your skills up to date is a habit, not a task. A trainee who learns one new skill every few months will be far ahead after two years.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: I can say what self-management means and why employers value it.
I can name my strengths and weaknesses, and ask for honest feedback.
I can reflect on a shift with: what went well, what to do better, what to change.
I can write short-term and long-term goals and a personal development plan with steps, help and dates.
I can keep copies of my certificates and a training record.
I can explain why punctuality and attendance matter, and what to do if I am sick or late.
I can plan a shift by putting urgent tasks first.
I can explain work ethic and integrity, with examples.
I can own up to a mistake and put it right.
I can follow instructions and procedures, ask questions and make suggestions properly.
I can tell initiative from going beyond my authority.
I can stay calm with a rude guest or an angry co-worker.
I can describe the signs of stress and healthy ways to deal with it.
I can respond to feedback calmly and make a plan to improve.
I can explain how sleep, food, water, hygiene and money affect my work.
I can accept change and keep my skills up to date.

c1.title: A busy morning at a villa in Treasure Beach
c1.text: Alicia is a villa attendant in Treasure Beach. Her task list for today: clean six bedrooms; set up a baby cot in Villa 2 for a family arriving at 1 p.m.; restock the linen store; and wash the pool-side towels. The guests in Villa 4 are leaving at 11 a.m., and a guest in Villa 3 phones to ask for extra towels now. Her supervisor, Mr Bailey, is out collecting supplies until noon.

c2.title: Orville and the 7 a.m. shift
c2.text: Orville works at a hotel in Montego Bay. His shift starts at 7 a.m. He normally takes a route taxi at 6:15 a.m. One morning he wakes at 5:30 a.m. with a fever and a headache and does not feel fit to work. Another time, his taxi breaks down at 6:40 a.m., and he knows he will be about 20 minutes late. The hotel's rule is that staff phone their supervisor before the shift starts to report sickness or lateness.

c3.title: A forgotten order at the restaurant
c3.text: Joel is a server in a hotel restaurant in Ocho Rios. During a busy dinner he forgets to enter a table's main courses into the order system. After 25 minutes the guests complain loudly and one of them says the service is a disgrace. A co-worker, Shanique, says to Joel in front of other staff, 'You always let us down.' Joel feels his face go hot and his heart racing.

c4.title: Michelle's appraisal
c4.text: Michelle is a room attendant at a hotel in Montego Bay. At her appraisal, her supervisor tells her that guests praise her friendliness and her rooms are always ready on time. However, room checks found dust under the beds and an empty soap dish in three rooms. Michelle is tired because she works a second job at night, and she has been spending her pay as soon as she gets it. She wants to become a floor supervisor in two years.

c5.title: Long days at a beach bar in Negril
c5.text: Ryan is a bartender at a beach bar in Negril. He works from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. in full sun, and on his days off he stays up late. He sleeps about four hours a night, drinks mostly sweet soda during his shift and skips lunch when it is busy. Last week he spilled a tray of drinks and nearly cut his hand on a broken glass. On pay day he spends most of his pay at a party and is short of money by the middle of the month.

questions.q: In what order should Alicia plan her morning?
o: Villa 3's towels now, Villa 4 once it is empty, the cot in Villa 2, then the other rooms
The linen store first, then the pool-side towels, and then all the bedrooms in number order, then any requests
The bedrooms she finds easiest first, and any guest requests when she has some time left over later
Wait for Mr Bailey to return at noon and ask him how she should plan the rest of her day
questions.why: Self-management means putting guest requests and time-critical tasks first: the towels are needed now, the cot is needed before 1 p.m. and Villa 4 can be cleaned once it is empty. Restocking and washing can wait.

questions.q: While cleaning, Alicia notices that the baby cot in the store has a loose screw. What is the best action?
o: Put the cot aside, tag it as faulty and report it before the family arrives
Tighten the screw herself with a screwdriver from the store, then set the cot up for the family
Set the cot up as planned and ask the family to check the screw before they use it for the baby
Leave it in the store and let the next shift find out about the loose screw when they need it
questions.why: A faulty item for a baby is a safety risk, and there is a procedure for reporting faulty equipment. Alicia should not repair it without training or permission, and should not give it to guests.

questions.q: Alicia finishes her rooms early, and the pool deck has litter on it. What does initiative look like here?
o: Clear the litter, then tell Mr Bailey what she has done
Wait until Mr Bailey notices the litter and asks someone else to clear it away
Add some pool chemicals to clear the water too, since she has spare time
Take a long break, since all of her own tasks on the list are now completed
questions.why: Clearing litter is within her role and safe. Initiative means seeing what needs doing and doing it. Pool chemicals need training and are outside her authority.

questions.q: A guest in Villa 3 asks Alicia to move her to a larger villa that is free. What should Alicia do?
o: Explain politely that approval is needed, and ask Mr Bailey or the front office
Move her at once, to keep the guest happy and to avoid any complaint later
Tell her the larger villa is not available, to avoid any more questions from her
Tell her she may move herself, and say that Alicia will carry the bags later
questions.why: Moving a guest changes bookings and rates, which is a supervisor's decision. Alicia should be polite, say she will check, and pass the request on, instead of promising or refusing.

questions.q: Orville wakes with a fever. What should he do?
o: Phone his supervisor before 7 a.m., say he is sick and when he expects to return
Send a text to a co-worker and ask her to pass the news on to the supervisor
Stay home and explain when he comes in again at the end of the week
Go to work anyway and handle the guests' food, so that he is not missed by anyone
questions.why: Follow the property's rule: call early, before the shift, so cover can be arranged. Staying away without telling anyone is a serious fault, and working sick near food or rooms can spread illness.

questions.q: The taxi breaks down and Orville will be 20 minutes late. What is the best response?
o: Phone his supervisor at once, with the reason and the time he will arrive
Arrive at 7:20 a.m. and explain what happened when his supervisor asks him
Wait until he reaches the hotel and then tell the supervisor in person what happened
Tell his co-workers on social media that he will be late for today's shift
questions.why: Phoning before the start time lets the supervisor cover his work. Telling the supervisor in advance shows reliability, even though he is still late.

questions.q: How could Orville make his route-taxi problems less likely to make him late?
o: Leave home earlier and plan to arrive 10 to 15 minutes before the shift
Leave at the same time as now and hope that the taxis will run on time
Ask his supervisor to start his shift later on the days when taxis are slow
Change jobs to one that starts at a time that suits the route taxis better
questions.why: Punctuality means being ready at the start of the shift. Leaving early gives time for delays. Self-managed workers solve the problem themselves instead of expecting the shift to change.

questions.q: The guests complain loudly. What should Joel do first?
o: Take a slow breath, apologise and say what he will do to put it right
Explain that the kitchen is always slow on Friday nights, so it was not his fault
Tell them the order system was down, to explain the long wait for their meals
Ask them to speak more quietly, since other guests in the restaurant can hear them
questions.why: Joel should stay calm, take responsibility and offer action. Blaming the kitchen or the system, or telling guests how to behave, makes the situation worse.

questions.q: What should Joel do about the mistake itself?
o: Enter the order now, tell the supervisor and the kitchen, and ask for it to be rushed
Enter the order and say nothing more, hoping the guests will not mention it again
Tell the supervisor the kitchen lost the order, so that the guests will get a free dessert
Give the guests a free drink from the bar, without telling anyone else what has happened
questions.why: Own up quickly, put the order right by the procedure and tell the supervisor, who can decide on any compensation. Joel cannot decide on free items himself and should not blame the kitchen.

questions.q: Shanique speaks to him unkindly in front of other staff. What is the best way for Joel to handle it?
o: Finish the service calmly, then ask to talk to her in private
Reply sharply there and then, so that she knows not to speak to him that way
Refuse to work with her for the rest of the night, to show that he is upset
Tell the guests at his tables about her behaviour, so that they understand what happened
questions.why: Do not argue in front of guests or staff. Finish the work, then talk privately and calmly using 'I' statements. If it does not work, speak to the supervisor.

questions.q: Later Joel thinks about why he forgot the order. What is the most useful action for him?
o: Enter each table's order before moving on, and check his list after each round
Decide to avoid busy shifts, so that he does not make this kind of mistake again
Decide that mistakes are normal, and that he does not need to change anything he does
Decide to take fewer tables, even when the restaurant is fully booked for the night
questions.why: Learning from a mistake means finding the cause and changing your routine. Avoiding busy shifts or doing nothing does not solve the problem.

questions.q: Michelle's supervisor says the rooms have dust under the beds. What is the best response?
o: Listen calmly, ask to be shown what is expected, and plan to check under the beds
Explain that the guests were happy and that nobody complained about the dust at all
Say that the last supervisor never checked under the beds, so she did not know to do it
Say that she has too many rooms to clean to be able to check under every single bed
questions.why: Constructive feedback is information to improve with. Arguing or making excuses blocks learning. Michelle should ask questions, practise, and ask to be checked again.

questions.q: Which of these would be a short-term goal for Michelle?
o: To pass every room check for the next month, with no missed items
To become a floor supervisor at this hotel in two years' time
To finish NVQ-J Level 3 at some point in the future when she can
To be known as the best room attendant in the whole hotel one day
questions.why: A short-term goal is clear, measurable and has a near date. Becoming a supervisor in two years is a long-term goal, and the other two have no clear date or measure.

questions.q: Michelle's tiredness is probably a cause of her missed checks. What should she do?
o: Look at her sleep and time off, and tell her supervisor she is tired
Say nothing to anyone, and work faster to try to make up for the lost time
Stop checking the rooms so carefully, so that she can finish on time each day
Ask the supervisor to give her fewer rooms, but to keep paying her the same
questions.why: Tiredness causes mistakes. Self-management means looking honestly at the cause and talking about it. Hiding the problem or reducing checks makes things worse.

questions.q: Michelle wants to be a floor supervisor and spends her pay as soon as she gets it. What is the best first step?
o: Plan her spending, save a little each pay day, and list the training she needs
Wait to be noticed and promoted, since supervisors are chosen by their managers
Ask for a pay rise before she has improved her room checks at the hotel
Spend only on things for her future job, and stop paying her other bills
questions.why: Money worries affect work and health. Planning spending and saving, and working on a development plan with training goals, are within her control.

questions.q: Which change would help Ryan most to work safely in the heat?
o: Drink water often, wear a hat, take breaks in the shade and eat lunch
Drink more sweet soda for energy, and skip lunch only on the busiest days
Take off his shirt and hat to keep cool while he works behind the bar
Drink strong energy drinks through the shift to stay alert until closing time
questions.why: Working outside all day without water, food or sun protection can cause faintness and heat exhaustion. Sweet drinks and energy drinks do not replace water.

questions.q: Ryan sleeps four hours a night. How is this likely to affect his work?
o: He is more likely to make mistakes and have accidents, like spills
He will work faster, because he has more time awake to serve the guests
It will make no difference, since he is young and strong enough to manage
He will only feel tired on his days off, and not during the shifts he works
questions.why: Most adults need about seven to nine hours' sleep. Tired workers slow down, forget things and have accidents. Ryan's spill and near cut are warnings.

questions.q: Ryan's pay is gone by mid-month. What would be a good self-management step?
o: Write down his pay and fixed costs, and save a set amount each pay day
Borrow money each month from a lender who charges a very high interest rate
Ask his co-workers to lend him money every month until the next pay day comes
Ask his supervisor for his pay to be paid later in the month instead
questions.why: Planning how you spend your pay is part of self-management. High-interest loans make problems worse, and depending on others to lend money is not a plan.

questions.q: A famous singer asks the villa staff to keep his stay secret, and a co-worker wants to post a photo with him online. What should you do?
o: Ask the co-worker not to post it, as it breaks the guest's privacy
Post it, since the singer is famous and probably likes the attention it would bring
Say nothing, since what staff post in their free time is nobody else's business
Ask the singer to sign the photo first, then post it with his name on it
questions.why: Guests' privacy comes first, and posts about guests can harm the business. A professional respects the guest's wish, whoever the guest is.

questions.q: Your supervisor shows you a new way to enter orders on the computer, and you find it confusing. What is the best action?
o: Practise when it is quiet and ask for help when you are stuck
Keep writing orders by hand, and let the others use the new system for now
Wait for the new system to break, so that the old way comes back again
Ask a co-worker to enter all of your orders into it for you each shift
questions.why: A flexible, self-managed worker accepts change and learns it. Practising and asking for help shows a positive attitude, and avoiding the system shifts your work to others.
